endings.text: End of the walk. After a bitter fight, early in 1905, the husband won: the divorce, the house on Prairie Avenue and the custody of the boy. On 8 March 1905 he sold the house to Charles Palmerston Anderson, the Episcopal bishop of Chicago. That same week the Tribune found Catherine Brown in a police cell, arrested at 3667 Wabash Avenue, where the police said she had been living as Kittie Casey, and fined $85. "I am penniless," she said. "I cannot pay the fine." In her cell she said: "It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess." The general's daughter from Buffalo had held 1612 Prairie for less than a year.

evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 22 February 1884, 'Wedding Bells', as transcribed.
evidence.text: On 21 February 1884 about 200 of the intimate friends and relatives of the bride and groom were received at the residence of W. F. Studebaker, No. 1612 Prairie avenue, after the Studebaker-Innis wedding. 'The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers.'

Inter Ocean, 2 January 1887: 'Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals.' Its owner was one of the Studebaker Brothers, the carriage makers.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.
evidence.text: Catherine G. Brown was the 'former wife of Charles E. Brown, 1612 Prairie avenue'. Mrs. Brown, who is 27 years old and the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo, first attracted notoriety in May, 1904, when her husband filed a bill for divorce. By a court order issued by Judge Tuley Mrs. Brown was given possession of the residence, 1612 Prairie avenue, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and was granted temporary alimony amounting to $200 a month while the suit was pending. Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges were the grounds.
Joseph Goodman Residence, 1612 S. Prairie Avenue: razed circa 1960.

evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.
evidence.text: In November Mr. Brown appeared in court and charged that his wife had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe.

He also charged her with receiving the attentions of E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman. With Edsall, the husband charged, Mrs. Brown ran away to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City.

evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, the last paragraph, as transcribed.
evidence.text: After a bitter fight Mr. Brown was granted a divorce about six weeks before 11 March 1905, and given possession of the Prairie avenue property, and the custody of the one son, Charles Edward Brown.

In March 1905 Mrs. Catherine G. Brown was arrested at 3667 Wabash avenue, where she had been living under the name of Kittie Casey, according to the police, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. 'I am penniless,' she said. 'I cannot pay the fine.' In her cell she said: 'It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess.' Justice Hurley called her 'a problem in humanity to me.'

evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 14 March 1905, the transfer list, as transcribed.
evidence.text: On 8 March 1905 the lot at 1612 Prairie passed from Brown (printed 'Chas. S. Brown') to the Rt. Rev. Chas. Palmerston Anderson, bishop of the Protestant Episcopal church in the diocese of Chicago.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SCANDAL AT 1612 PRAIRIE. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the quiet north end of Prairie Avenue.

Four stops along one short block. The house at 1612 has been a showplace for twenty years. This year it is a battlefield. A husband has gone to court, a judge has handed the house to the wife, and in November the husband stood up in open court and said things about her that the whole city has now read in the Tribune. The neighbours keep their curtains closed and their ears open.

Start next door, where you can see the house the way it used to be.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

dexter_house_1721_prairie_frame_house.text: Wirt Dexter's frame house of 1863, the first house on this lot. Arthur Little's brick front on Prairie Avenue was built onto its street end; the old house's own front, porch and bay windows, faces the side yard.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

hibbard_house_1701_prairie.text: William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, by William Le Baron Jenney, who fifteen years later built the Home Insurance Building, called the first skyscraper.

high_house_2021_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James L. High here.

house_1600_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists John G. Shortall here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

house_1608_prairie.text: The Frank household. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the Chicago Woman's Club in 1876.

house_1616_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William R. Stirling here.

house_1619_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Howard E. Perry here, a clerk by the 1900 census. Before them, Walter H. Wilson lived here (1891).

jones_house_1834_prairie.text: A brick Italianate house by John M. Van Osdel, built in 1866 for Fernando Jones, one of Chicago's earliest settlers. In 1886 it gained a mansard roof, to keep up with its neighbors.

keith_house_1808_prairie.text: Osborn R. Keith's granite-fronted house of 1886 by Cobb and Frost, noticed that year at forty thousand dollars, going up as Richardson's granite house rose next door.

kellogg_house_1709_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Jesse Spalding here, a lumberman by the 1900 census. Before them, Mrs. Palmer V. Kellogg lived here (1890-1893).

kellogg_house_1923_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. C. P. Kellogg here. Before them, Pierrepont Isham lived here (1895-1899).

kimball_house_1801_prairie.text: A house in the French château style, built in 1890 for William W. Kimball. He made pianos and organs. Solon S. Beman was the architect.

law_house_1620_prairie.text: Robert Law's house, engraved in 1874 for a series on the homes of Chicago: two storeys over a raised basement under a slated mansard.

marsh_house_1824_prairie.text: Samuel B. Pomeroy's Italianate villa of 1857, one of the oldest houses on the street, hiding behind the stone front George B. Marsh gave it after 1880.

marshall_field_house_1905_prairie.text: Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal. Field is the wealthiest businessman in Chicago, and the street's most famous neighbour.

marshall_field_jr_house_1919_prairie.text: Built in 1867 and made bigger several times. Marshall Field Jr. bought it in 1890. In 1902 D. H. Burnham and Company added a huge new part.

mayer_house_2009_prairie.text: Max A. Meyer's house of 1888, a French Gothic rowhouse by Burnham and Root.

moulton_lowden_house_1912_prairie.text: A big house in the French château style, built in 1882 for B. P. Moulton. In 1898 Frank O. Lowden moved in. He later became governor of Illinois.

otis_house_2033_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists F. R. Otis here.

pullman_house_1729_prairie.text: George M. Pullman's mansion, built between 1870 and 1876. Inside were a theatre for about 200 people, a pipe organ and a bowling alley.

ream_house_1901_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Norman B. Ream here, a capitalist by the 1900 census.

rees_house_2110_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edson Keith jr. here. Before them, Mrs. James H. Rees lived here (1890-1892).

robbins_house_2126_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Edward F. Robbins here. Before them, the Hamill household lived here (1890-1899).

roloson_house_2109_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert W. Roloson here. Before them, Mrs. Judith L. Marshall lived here (1890-1899).

rothschild_house_2112_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. M. M. Rothschild here.

sears_meeker_house_1815_prairie.text: Built for Joseph Sears; by 1904 the Blue Book lists Arthur Meeker here.

sherman_house_2100_prairie.text: Built in 1874 for John B. Sherman, who ran the Union Stock Yards. Burnham and Root were the architects. Sherman's daughter Margaret married Daniel Burnham while it was going up.

shortall_gregory_house_1638_prairie_fron.text: Built in 1868. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Robert B. Gregory here.

spalding_house_1637_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists William Gold Hibbard jr. here. Before them, the Spalding household lived here (1890-1899).

tucker_smith_house_2140_prairie.text: Built in 1876. In 1904 the Blue Book lists Byron L. Smith here.

walker_house_1720_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. James M. Walker here. Before them, Miss Jennie Royce lived here (1890-1891).

wheeler_house_1812_prairie.text: A brick row house in the Dutch style, built in 1884 for George H. Wheeler. He owned grain elevators. Burnham and Root designed it.

premise: A carriage-maker's showplace has become the most talked-about house on the block: a society divorce, a judge's order, a violin in a broken automobile, and a small boy in the middle of it all.

stage.caption: A maid at 1608 sweeps her steps and keeps one eye on the house next door.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, and beside it the big square house at 1612. Twenty years ago it belonged to a Studebaker, of the Studebaker Brothers carriage works, and it was the brightest house on the street. In February 1884 some two hundred guests came here from a family wedding, and "The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers." A society column of 1887 noticed the traffic: "Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals." A carriage-maker's house should have the finest carriages at its door, and it did. Look at it now. No turnout stands at the curb this afternoon. A maid from next door is watching it from her steps. Walk to the gate of 1612.

stage.caption: A lady comes out onto the steps of 1612, looks up and down the street, and goes back in before anyone can stop her.

cast.name: Catherine G. Brown (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays her)

stops.text: 1612 Prairie. The Tribune has the story, and so does everybody else. Last May the husband, Charles E. Brown, filed a bill for divorce. His wife Catherine is 27, "the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo". The grounds were "Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges". Then Judge Tuley gave Mrs. Brown possession of this house, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and $200 a month while the suit was pending. So the wife holds the fortress and the husband is outside it. Behind those windows live a woman the papers have made famous and a small boy. The house will stand until it is razed circa 1960. Step next door and hear what the husband said in November.

stage.caption: Two maids on the steps of 1616 share the newspaper and look over at 1612.

stops.text: 1616 Prairie, the next door south, where the neighbours read the Tribune with their coffee. In November Mr. Brown went back to court and charged that his wife "had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe." There was more. He named a man: "E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman." With Edsall, the husband charged, she ran off to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City. It is the most delicious scandal on Prairie Avenue in years, and two maids on these steps are making the most of it. But a divorce is not only about two people. Look for the boy.

stage.caption: A nurse walks a small boy along the far sidewalk past the door of 1612, and he stops to look up at it.

cast.name: Charles Edward Brown, the son (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays him)
A nurse of the Brown household (unnamed)

stops.text: Across the street at 1613, look back at the west side of the block. The boy is Charles Edward Brown, the couple's only son, and he is the real prize in this fight. A nurse walks him along the sidewalk past his own front door; his mother has the house, and his father wants it back, and wants him. The court has not decided. In the newspapers he is a line at the end of every story. On this walk he is the only person in the whole affair who has done nothing at all. The Tribune will report the end of it in March 1905. By then the house, the boy and the woman will each have gone a different way.

title: The Scandal at 1612 Prairie
